# Every Man in the Trap {#types-of-user}

> "God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men"
>
> — a Pharisee at prayer, Luke 18:11

Men who masturbate every day tend to envy the man who doesn't. We've all met him, or read his posts. "Honestly, I can go a couple of weeks and not even think about it." We wish we were built like that.

Don't. This may be hard to believe, but no man in the trap enjoys being in it, however lightly he seems to wear it. Keep three things in view:

- No man ever decided to get hooked, lightly or heavily.
- So every man in the trap feels like a fool.
- So every man in the trap has to lie, to himself and to everyone else, to make it look like a choice.

Think about how people talk about things they really enjoy. A serious fisherman tells you how often he gets out on the water, and wishes it were more. So why does a man boast about how *little* he does it? If going without is the thing to be proud of, the trophy belongs to the man who never does it at all.

Suppose a friend said to you, "I can go two whole weeks without toast, and it doesn't bother me in the slightest." You'd wonder what was wrong with him. If he likes toast, why go without? If he doesn't, why mention it? A man only makes a speech like that about something that has a hold on him. What the two-week man is really telling you is: "I survived two weeks." Like every man in the trap, he's hoping that if he can survive two weeks he might one day survive for good. And if two weeks was a feat of survival, imagine how precious the next time must have been.

That's why the man who does it rarely is, in one way, more firmly caught than the man who does it daily. The illusion of pleasure is bigger for him, because he's always coming off a long wait. He also has less reason to get out. It costs him less time, and the damage is harder to see. Things do go wrong: a flat mood, a wandering mind in bed with his partner, a coldness when he tries to pray. He puts them down to work or tiredness or his age.

## Why every man doesn't do it all day {-}

If you've got an itch that never quite goes, the natural thing is to scratch whenever it nags. Each scratch works a little less well than the one before. So the natural drift is always toward more: more often, for longer, with stronger material. So why isn't every man in the trap doing it five times a day? Four things hold him back.

1. **Time.** He has a job, a family and a life, and most days are full.
2. **The body.** It has limits. A man can only go so many rounds, and those limits change with his age, his health and how tired he is. It's an automatic brake.
3. **Privacy.** A partner in the bed, a roommate, children who don't knock, thin walls. For many men the only thing between them and twice as often is a lack of locked doors.
4. **Conscience.** The tug of war that goes on in every man in the trap. Some of it comes from how he was raised, some from a partner's opinion, and some from a plain dislike of what he's turning into.

Men who do it daily tend to think of themselves as weak, and can't see how other men keep it to once a week. But the once-a-week man is usually no stronger. One or more of those four brakes is simply on harder. He shares a small apartment, or he's fifty-five, or he works fourteen-hour days. Take the brake off, say with a week alone in a hotel, and watch what he does.

Now some types. Find yourself in the list. You may be in it more than once.

## The ladder {-}

- **The man who never started.** He's rare, and he shouldn't be smug about it. He's outside the trap by upbringing, luck or the grace of God. Every man inside it was once sure he'd never be caught.
- **The beginner.** He's usually a boy of twelve or thirteen. Don't envy him. He's a fly strolling about on the rim of the jar. Every nightly man started out as an occasional one.
- **The nightly man.** Once a day, in bed, lights off. He calls it his sleeping pill. He eases his itch for ten minutes in every twenty-four hours and carries it for the rest. He walks all day with a stone in his shoe so that he can enjoy taking it out at bedtime.
- **The streak counter.** You met him in the chapter on willpower. When he's doing it, he wishes he weren't. When he's stopped, he feels deprived and counts the days. He has the worst of both. His cousin, the retention monk, is stopping in order to get something: a deeper voice, a glow, women's heads turning. He has only swapped one kind of counting for another.
- **The man on porn.** This is the heavy end, and most men in the trap have spent time here. The screen never runs out, so he loses hours where another man loses minutes. He ends up watching things that would have sickened him at eighteen. He isn't a monster. The way out is the same for him, and it is no harder.
- **The man who quit porn and kept the hand.** He tells himself it's a different thing now. He has only cut down. He's still feeding the same Little Monster, and on some bad night the monster will remember where the stronger food is kept.
- **The man led by women.** His lust goes out through real women. He follows, flatters, pays and waits. Or he lives on the dating apps, swiping every night and meeting nobody. Or he's married and keeps a "harmless" flirtation going at work. He thinks nothing has happened. Ask his wife whether nothing has happened.
- **The collector.** He goes from bed to bed and keeps count. He gets a section of his own in a moment.
- **The man who pays.** He would never go to a prostitute. But he pays a monthly fee to see one woman's private pictures, and he tips her so that she will write back. Or he sends money to a woman who plays video games on a live stream, so that she will say his name. Or it's the strip club, or the massage parlor with the back room. Young men have a word for this man. They call him a simp, a man who pays a woman for attention she will never return. It is a big business. In 2024, men spent more than seven billion dollars on the largest of these subscription sites. And here is what that money often buys. Reporters found that many of the women there never write the messages at all. Agencies hire workers to do it, called chatters. Many of them are men, sitting in offices on the other side of the world, paid to type like her and to keep him spending. He thinks he has a girlfriend. He is a customer, and he is being worked. If this is you, add up what you have paid this year and look at the number. Then cancel the subscription and block the page tonight.
- **The man with a machine.** This one is new. He talks every night to a girlfriend made by a computer. She is always awake and always pleased with him. She never has a bad day and never says no. Or he has the computer make pictures of women to his order. In one American survey, nearly a third of young men said they had chatted with a machine as a boyfriend or girlfriend. Of those who had, one in five said they liked it better than talking to a real person. This is the harem of imaginary brides with a voice added. It is the prison C.S. Lewis warned about, and now the walls talk back.
- **The man who "only reads".** He doesn't watch videos. He reads sex stories, or he looks at drawings and cartoons, which the internet calls hentai, a Japanese word. "No real woman is involved", he says. But the lust is real, and it is his. Jesus put the sin in the heart, and the heart is the same whether the page holds a photograph or a drawing.
- **The single man who'll stop when he's married.** Ask any married man how that went. A wedding doesn't end the itch. "When I'm married" is the most comfortable way there is of saying "not yet". If you intend to give a woman your whole self one day, the kindest thing you can do for her is to arrive already free.

Five men need more than a line.

## The collector {-}

There's a man who keeps a number. He wouldn't tell his mother, but he knows it exactly. The men online call it a body count, and they compare numbers the way boys compare scores.

Ask him about the women and something odd comes out. He didn't like half of them. Some he wasn't even attracted to. He slept with them anyway, because each one moved the number up. And the number told him something he badly needed to hear: women want you, so you must be somebody.

That isn't confidence. It's a man so unsure of his worth that he needs a new woman every few days to vote on it.

Picture a man at a buffet for the first time. He stacks plate after plate. He paid a lot to get in and he may never be back, so he takes everything. Now watch the wealthy man at the same buffet. He takes what he wants and leaves the rest. He isn't afraid it will run out. The man who takes every woman who offers is not the rich man in that room. He's the hungry one.

Now try something. Suppose every night like that came with what sex was built to carry. If you sleep with her, you stay with her. You marry her. If a child comes, that child is a human life, and yours to raise. And you'll spend far more of your years talking with her, eating with her and sitting through her bad days than you will ever spend in bed with her.

Would you still have gone home with her?

Most men answer at once. "No. Not her." Then she was never someone you wanted. She was a plate.

Here is a question for any man, believer or not. If you had lived as though the Christian rules were true, would you have made better decisions, or worse?


## The man led by a woman {-}

The internet calls it simping. A man wants a woman so badly that she can lead him anywhere, and so can anyone else who knows what he wants. It is a very old problem. The Bible tells it twice.

The first man is Samson, in the book of Judges. He was the strongest man who ever lived. God gave him that strength to free his people from their enemies, the Philistines, and no army could hold him. His weakness was women, and his enemies knew it. He fell in love with a woman named Delilah, and the Philistine rulers came to her with an offer. "Entice him, and see in which his great strength lies." Each of them promised her eleven hundred pieces of silver.

So she asked him. "Please tell me where your great strength lies." He told her a lie. Tie me with seven fresh cords, he said, and I'll be as weak as any man. She tied him with them, with men hiding in the next room, and shouted, "The Philistines are on you, Samson!" He snapped the cords like thread. She asked again, and he lied again. This time it was new ropes, and the same thing happened. She asked a third time, and it happened a third time.

Stop there and look at him. Three times this woman has tried to hand him to men who want him dead. He knows it. He has seen the ropes. And he stays. That is what lust does to a strong man's judgment. He isn't fooled. He just can't leave.

Then she used the oldest line there is. "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me?" She "pressed him daily with her words" until he was worn out, and at last he told her the truth.

His strength was tied to a vow he had been under since birth. It was called the Nazirite vow, a vow of special dedication to God, and its sign was that his hair had never been cut. She put him to sleep on her knees, called a man to shave his head, and collected her silver.

He woke up sure that he would shake himself free as before. "But he didn't know that the LORD had departed from him." The Philistines put out his eyes, the eyes that had led him all his life, "and he ground at the mill in the prison".

But the story doesn't end at the mill. The very next line reads, "However, the hair of his head began to grow again".

The Philistine rulers held a great feast for their god, Dagon, to celebrate the capture. Thousands of people filled the temple, and they had Samson brought up from the prison to entertain them. A boy led him by the hand, because he couldn't see. Samson asked to be put where he could feel the two pillars that held the building up.

Then he prayed. "Lord GOD, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once".

God heard him. Samson pushed with all his might, and the temple came down on the rulers and on himself. The Bible says he killed more of his people's enemies in his death than in his whole life.

It isn't a tidy ending. He was praying for revenge for his eyes, and it cost him his life. He never got back his sight or the wasted years. But God heard a ruined man when he asked, and gave him back the work he was born for. Centuries later the New Testament lists the heroes of faith, and Samson's name is on the list.

If you have been at the mill for years, he still hears that prayer.

The second man is King Ahab. He married a foreign princess named Jezebel, a ruthless woman, and he let her run him. Ahab wanted a vineyard beside his palace. The owner, Naboth, wouldn't sell. So the king of Israel went home, lay on his bed, turned his face to the wall and refused to eat. Jezebel found him sulking. "Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel?" she said. She wrote letters in his name, sealed them with his seal, and had Naboth killed on a false charge. Then she told her husband to go and take his vineyard, and he went.

Ahab never gave the order. He only wanted something badly, and let someone else use his seal. The Bible doesn't excuse him. It says he "sold himself", and that his wife "stirred up" what was already in him. When a prophet confronted him, Ahab tore his clothes and fasted, and God held the disaster back. But it didn't last. Three years later he was jailing a prophet for telling him the truth, and he died in battle.

So the two stories end differently. Samson lost nearly everything and turned back to God at the end. Ahab was sorry for a while and then went on as before.

Being sorry is not the same as turning around.

And notice where both stories put the blame. Delilah was paid and Jezebel was ruthless. But Samson gave away his own secret, and Ahab handed over his own seal. A man ruled by what he wants ends up ruled by whoever can give it to him.

## The married man {-}

He thought the wedding would end it. Many of us did. He found out within the month that it had come with him on the honeymoon.

He believes he's owed a release every day or two. His wife is not always of the same mind. She's tired, or pregnant, or away, or they've had a fight. So he "fills the gap". Her tiredness is never his excuse, and the habit doesn't stay inside the gap anyway. Soon it's happening on nights when she would have said yes, because it's quicker, because it asks nothing, because nobody has to be wooed. In time he's half glad when she turns over, since it hands him his excuse.

And when she does reach for him, he's already spent, or his mind is on a reel she isn't in. He gave the best of it to nobody, and she gets what's left over.

If the habit really gave a man so much, he wouldn't need a wife. It gives nothing, and it takes from her. One husband wrote, after he finally saw it:

> "I was beside myself over how I had grieved God and my wife"

Whatever you believe about marriage, you promised her this part of yourself. A man who takes it back in secret, a little at a time, is keeping something from her. Some part of her knows it, even if she couldn't tell you what's wrong.

## The "imagination only" man {-}

"I don't look at anything. It's all in my head."

Everybody starts there. Isn't it strange how the scenes don't stay tame? Last year's picture stops working, so the mind supplies something a little further on. Then it wants a real face: a coworker, a friend's wife, the girl who serves your coffee. Then it wants "just a photo, to get started". We traced that road in the chapter on the flesh.

For nearly every man, though, the head is far from empty, and you knew that already. The imagination-only man is proud that no one else's sin is on his screen. But he's the director, the casting agent and the whole audience of his own private movie theater, and the women in it never agreed to appear.

Worst of all is the husband who believes he's safe because he only ever pictures his wife. He's still teaching his body that the finish line is himself, alone, on his own schedule. The version of her in his head never says "not like that" and never needs anything. Then he's puzzled that the real woman feels like harder work than she used to.

## The church guy who has never told anyone {-}

He serves on the welcome team, leads a small group, perhaps plays in the band. He has done this since he was fourteen and has never said one word about it to a living soul.

On Sunday he's at the front with his hands raised. On Saturday night he was where he always is. He has confessed it so many times, in the same words, that he's embarrassed to bring it up with God again. So he's stopped bringing it up, and after a while he's stopped bringing much else up either.

Peter once asked Jesus how many times he had to forgive his brother. Seven times? Jesus said seventy times seven. God doesn't hold himself to a lower standard than the one he gave Peter.

It leaks into everything he might have done. He turns down the mission trip, lets someone else lead, and never says why. He is enlisted, and he keeps reporting sick.

The church guy has one burden the others don't. He believes he's the only one. He looks down the row at the other men and assumes they're all clean. They're looking back down the row at him and assuming the same. The habit is feeding on that silence, and there's a whole chapter on it shortly.

You don't need to envy any of them, and you don't need to be one. Life is simply better outside. Here is a nineteen-year-old who got out:

> "From that moment on, I began rejoicing that Jesus had delivered me from this 5 year addiction"

He didn't write that he was managing it, or that he'd reached day ninety. He wrote that he'd been delivered, and that he was rejoicing.

Which brings us back to the prayer this chapter opened with: "God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men". The man who prayed it was a Pharisee. The Pharisees were the strictest religious men of Jesus's day, and Jesus told a story about one of them, standing in the temple. Every type in this chapter says a version of that prayer. "At least I don't look at porn." "At least it's only once a week." "At least it's only in my head." "At least I've never cheated." "At least I'm not married yet." Jesus said the man who went home right with God that day was the other one. He was a tax collector, a man everyone despised. He compared himself with nobody. He only said, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!"

There aren't really any types. There's one trap, and men are standing at different depths in it. The way out is the same for all of them.
